around.headline: Woman loses Rs 4.5 lakh in gold to a bus 'pill-picking trick'
around.summary: A woman on a Bengaluru bus lost gold jewellery worth Rs 4.5 lakh to the classic 'pill-picking trick,' where a stranger uses a dropped pill or small object to distract a passenger while an accomplice steals valuables, per The Times of India. If someone in a crowded bus or auto points out an object on the floor near you, don't touch it or engage — just keep your hands on your bag and move away.

around.headline: Two-wheelers and autos banned on five elevated corridors from September 4
around.summary: Bengaluru traffic police are barring two-wheelers, autos and goods vehicles from five elevated roads and flyovers — including stretches near Electronic City and Airport Road — starting this Friday, per The Hindu, NDTV and CNBC-TV18. If your regular commute uses one of these corridors, plan an alternate route before Friday.

around.headline: KPCC protest at Freedom Park brings diversions to central Bengaluru today
around.summary: Traffic police have announced diversions and parking restrictions around Freedom Park for today's KPCC protest, per Deccan Herald. Avoid the area if you can, and expect slower traffic on nearby central routes through the day.

around.headline: BDA opens Karanth Layout site allotment after an 18-year wait
around.summary: The Bengaluru Development Authority has begun allotting sites in Dr. K. Shivaram Karanth Layout to original land losers at around ₹6,000/sq ft, with roughly 2,000 applications filed on day one, per The Hindu and Deccan Herald. Worth checking if you or a family member was among the original landowners still waiting on this allotment.

around.headline: GBA bans PoP Ganesh idols ahead of Gowri-Ganesha festival
around.summary: The Greater Bengaluru Authority has banned Plaster of Paris Ganesh idols ahead of the upcoming Gowri-Ganesha festival, while clearing eco-friendly clay idols for use, per ThePrint and The Times of India. If you're buying an idol this year, check that it's clay, not PoP, to avoid it being turned away at immersion points.

around.headline: Food safety raid seizes Rs 5.99 lakh of adulterated sweets in Bengaluru
around.summary: A food safety drive raided sweet manufacturing units across Karnataka, seizing Rs 5.99 lakh worth of stock over labelling and hygiene violations, per Bangalore Mirror and The Hindu. With festival season approaching, it's worth buying sweets from outlets that display valid FSSAI licences rather than the cheapest stall.

around.headline: IMD warns of heavy to extremely heavy rain in several states as Nepal flood toll passes 1,050
around.summary: The India Meteorological Department has issued heavy-to-extremely-heavy rainfall warnings for several states, even as the death toll from Nepal's flash floods crosses 1,050, per Inshorts and The Hindu. Bengaluru's own 71% rain chance today is part of the same active weather system, so keep an eye on evening commute conditions.

street_smart.title: You're on a crowded BMTC bus when the passenger next to you bends down, picks up a small pill-like object off the floor near your feet, and asks if it's yours or if you can help figure out what it is — like today's Bengaluru case where a woman lost gold jewellery worth Rs 4.5 lakh to exactly this 'pill-picking trick.' What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: The Times of India, Sept 1 — 'Woman falls to pill-picking trick, loses gold jewellery worth Rs 4.5 lakh in bus.' This is the clearest choice-based trap in today's feeds; nothing else (traffic-ban pushback, a land allotment, a civic idol ban, a food-safety raid, or the Nepal floods) is a personal decision point the way this bus scam is. The evergreen rotation list is heavily used up in the last 3 weeks — rental traps (09-01), loan apps (08-31, 09-01), fake jobs (08-31), digital arrest (08-28), OTP scams (08-29), UPI fraud (08-26), cab overcharging (08-26), two-wheeler theft (08-27) — so a fresh news-based scenario was preferred over repeating any of those.
street_smart.situation: The bus is packed, you're standing with your bag and gold chain visible, and the person seems genuinely puzzled about the object rather than aggressive — which is exactly what makes the approach work.

choices.text: Say it's not yours, keep both hands on your bag and jewellery, and move to another part of the bus or get off at the next stop if they keep pressing.
choices.feedback: Correct. The 'pill-picking trick' only works if you engage — the moment you touch the object, ask questions, or let it hold your attention, you've created the split-second window an accomplice needs to lift jewellery, unclasp a chain, or swap a bag. Disengaging immediately and putting distance between you and the pair removes that window entirely.

choices.text: Pick it up to see what it is and ask around the bus if anyone else dropped it.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. The object itself is bait — while you're bent over examining it or asking around, your hands are off your valuables and your attention is elsewhere, which is the exact moment an accomplice moves in to steal jewellery or swap your bag. The 'pill' is never actually about the pill.

choices.text: Ignore the object but stay in your seat and keep chatting with them since they seem friendly and harmless.
choices.feedback: Risky. Not touching the object helps, but staying engaged in conversation still keeps your guard down and your attention split — these tricks are built around a friendly, unthreatening approach specifically so you don't feel the need to disengage.

choices.text: Immediately grab the object and hand it to the conductor loudly, accusing the person of running a scam.
choices.feedback: Risky. You may be right, but confronting a stranger loudly on a moving, crowded bus with no proof can escalate fast and still means you've engaged directly instead of simply stepping away — the safer move is disengaging first, then alerting the conductor if you feel it's warranted.

takeaways: Never touch or examine an item a stranger points out to you in a bus, auto or crowd — Bengaluru's 'pill/tablet-picking' scams rely on that few seconds of distraction while an accomplice steals jewellery or bags.
On crowded public transport, keep gold chains and valuables tucked inside clothing or a zipped inner pocket rather than visible or loose.
If something goes missing, call 112 or report at the nearest police station right away, and note the bus number, route and time so BMTC/police can pull CCTV before it's overwritten.

quiz.question: From September 4, Bengaluru is banning two-wheelers and autos on how many elevated corridors and flyovers?
quiz.why: The ban covers stretches like Electronic City and Airport Road, and traffic police say it's meant to cut accidents on high-speed elevated roads.

quiz.question: BDA's new Dr. K. Shivaram Karanth Layout site allotment came after original land losers waited how many years?
quiz.why: Sites are priced at around ₹6,000/sq ft, and around 2,000 applications were filed on the very first day the allotment opened.

quiz.question: PM Modi made a strong comment on terrorism at which multilateral summit, with Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif present?
quiz.why: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation includes both India and Pakistan as members alongside China and Central Asian states, which is why the remark landed directly in front of Islamabad's delegation.

quiz.question: Which gas makes up roughly 78% of Earth's atmosphere by volume?
quiz.why: Oxygen is only about 21% of the atmosphere — nitrogen's abundance and inertness is why it's used to fill inert packaging and even some aircraft tyres.

quiz.question: What does the RBI's 'repo rate' refer to?
options: The interest rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks
The exchange rate RBI sets for the rupee
The minimum balance banks must keep with RBI
quiz.why: When RBI raises the repo rate, banks' own borrowing costs rise, and that usually gets passed on to you as higher EMIs on home and car loans.
